_note: Individuation: the definition (CW6 ¶757, ¶762), the becoming-in-dividual (CW7 ¶266, CW12 ¶330, CW9i ¶490), its two aspects (CW16 ¶448, CW7 ¶269), the aim and its cost (CW7 ¶405, CW14 ¶778, CW9i ¶705) and the dismantling it requires (CW7 ¶505). Quotations are placed by the corpus; nothing is typed.
line: Jung's definitions and statements on individuation (CW6, CW7, CW9i, CW12, CW16, CW14), with the passages that name its two aspects, its aim, and the two tensions the vault note records.

sections.title: The process
sections.line: CW6 ¶757, ¶758 and ¶762 (Definitions, 1921): the definition, and individuation as a natural necessity and as the development of consciousness out of the original state of identity.

quotes.quote: In general, it is the process by which individual beings are formed and differentiated; in particular, it is the development of the psychological individual (q.v.) as a being distinct from the general, collective psychology.
Individuation is practically the same as the development of consciousness out of the original state of identity
Individuation is a natural necessity inasmuch as its prevention by a levelling down to collective standards is injurious to the vital activity of the individual.

sections.title: Becoming an 'in-dividual'
sections.line: CW7 ¶266 (1928), CW12 ¶330 and CW9i ¶490: Jung's statements of what the word means, as in-dividual, as self and as whole.

quotes.quote: Individuation means becoming an “in-dividual,” and, in so far as “individuality” embraces our innermost, last, and incomparable uniqueness, it also implies becoming one’s own self.
In the last analysis every life is the realization of a whole, that is, of a self, for which reason this realization can also be called “individuation.”
that is, a separate, indivisible unity or "whole."

sections.title: Two aspects
sections.line: CW16 ¶448: the two principal aspects Jung names; CW7 ¶269: the aim of individuation as he states it against the persona and primordial images.

quotes.quote: Individuation has two principal aspects: in the first place it is an internal and subjective process of integration, and in the second it is an equally indispensable process of objective relationship
The aim of individuation is nothing less than to divest the self of the false wrappings of the persona on the one hand, and of the suggestive power of primordial images on the other

sections.title: The aim, and what it costs
sections.line: CW7 ¶405 on the goal of individuation, CW14 ¶778 on the experience of the self and the ego, CW9i ¶256 on its psychological meaning and CW9i ¶705 on the union of opposites.

quotes.quote: Sensing the self as something irrational, as an indefinable existent, to which the ego is neither opposed nor subjected, but merely attached, and about which it revolves very much as the earth revolves round the sun—thus we come to the goal of individuation.
For this reason the experience of the self is always a defeat for the ego
In its psychological meaning, individuation is an opus contra naturam
but the painful experience of the union of opposites.

sections.title: What it requires
sections.line: CW7 ¶505: the dissolution of the persona as an indispensable condition, and what Jung says of conscious intention.

quotes.quote: The dissolution of the persona is therefore an indispensable condition for individuation. It is, however, impossible to achieve individuation by conscious intention
